SUBJECT:  RECEIVE AND FILE  THE  ANNUAL  HOUSING  ELEMENT
  PROGRESS REPORT

ISSUE
Receive and file the summary of the Annual Housing Element Progress Report.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council receive and file the Annual Housing Element
Progress Report.

BACKGROUND
Government Code Section 65400 requires that all California cities provide an Annual
Housing Element Progress Report to the Governor’s Office of Planning and Research
(OPR) and the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD).
The intent of the statute is to describe the City’s progress in meeting its share of the
Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA). Also, by forwarding this report to
OPR and HCD the City may be eligible for future housing grants.

DISCUSSION
A total of 5,452 units have been allocated to the City of Palmdale during the planning
period October 2014 - October 2021 under its 5th cycle RHNA (Note: 6th cycle
RHNA allocations have been finalized but are not considered for this reporting period).

These units are distributed by affordability level and the Housing Element of the General
Plan must identify how the City plans to accommodate them. The City is required to
designate land for housing to ensure that there is enough residentially designated land
to meet its RHNA allocation, however, it is not required to ensure units are built. The City
is required to report on the progress of housing development in the form of the Annual
Housing Element Progress Report.

For calendar year 2020, there were 233 housing units issued a Certificate of Occupancy.
Table 1 provides a detail of Certificates issued for the past eight years.

The annual housing element report is not anticipated to have any fiscal impact.
However, the data within the report can be used to continue to streamline internal

Although no new revenue is anticipated, the construction of housing units of varied types

   City Council Staff Report
DATE:  MARCH 16, 2021
TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL
FROM:  ECONOMIC AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
  PLANNING DIVISION
DISTRICT:  ALL
SUBJECT:  RECEIVE UPDATE AND PROVIDE DIRECTION FOR THE
  GENERAL PLAN UPDATE PREFERRED LAND USE ALTERNATIVE

ISSUE
Receive an update on the preferred land use alternative for the General Plan (Palmdale
2045) update, review recommended changes resulting from community input and
provide feedback.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Receive an update on the General Plan Update (Palmdale 2045); and
  2. Provide feedback and direction on the preferred land use alternative.

BACKGROUND
Palmdale 2045 is a four-year project that commenced in January 2019 when the
City Council approved a professional services agreement with Raimi + Associates. The
General Plan serves as the City’s primary guide for land use and development decisions
and is a key tool for influencing and improving the quality of life for residents and
businesses. As such, it serves as the “blueprint” for future development and conservation
of a community. The General Plan will help the City plan for important community issues
such as new growth, housing needs and environmental protection. It also sets the stage
for future social, physical, and economic development of the City. It addresses issues
that impact the entire City, such as how land is used, where buildings are constructed,
and the locations of roads and parks.

DISCUSSION
The General Plan Team (GP Team) has worked with the General Plan Advisory
Committee (GPAC) to create the preferred land use alternative for public feedback as
well as review by the Planning Commission and City Council (ATTACHMENT 1).
TABLE 1 outlines the efforts undertaken since the GP Team presented to the City Council
in September 2020 with the three land use alternatives.

ANALYSIS
Existing Land Uses
The existing General Plan provides for primarily traditional suburban residential uses, with
regional-serving commercial developments found along 10th Street West and
47th Street East. The land use pattern does not provide for commercial nodes in
neighborhood-serving locations and contributes to urban sprawl, which in turn contributes
to increased reliance on individual use of automobiles. The General Plan focuses on
traditional commercial development, which discourages walkability and encourages large
expanses of street-facing parking. Although the land use pattern envisioned by the
existing General Plan was forward-thinking at the time of adoption, the General Plan has
not been comprehensively updated in 28 years and the type and location of land uses
specified within the General Plan do not maximize development potential or reflect current
best practices.

Land Use Framework
Based on research, constraints analysis, GPAC input, and the extensive community
visioning and feedback on issues and opportunities, the GP Team prepared a

  11
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: General Plan Preferred Land Use Alternative
March 16, 2021
Page 3

Land Use Framework that served as the foundation for three land use alternatives. The
Land Use Framework identifies areas of the City that could see major change as well as
areas of stability, that will largely remain the same. The GP Team then worked with the
GPAC to solidify areas of change and stability and prepare draft land use alternatives and
land use designations. The GP Team refined and further developed GPAC direction into
three stand-alone land use alternatives for comparison and input from the broader
community.

The Land Use Framework, included in the briefing book (ATTACHMENT 1), has been
further refined to encompass the entire City. Similarly, while the three land use
alternatives focused on areas of change, the preferred land use alternative covers the
entire City, including those areas that have unchanged land use designations.

The following section contains a brief description of the preferred land use alternative.

Preferred Land Use Alternative
As presented in September 2020, each of the three alternatives differed in the density
and location of housing and jobs, activity centers, and education and medical districts.
The three land use alternatives tested different land use and urban design patterns and
explained the trade-offs between each pattern to guide informed decisions.

After an extensive review of the alternatives with the community in July and August 2020,
the Planning Commission and City Council reviewed the alternatives and supplied
direction and additional feedback in September 2020. In general, Alternative 3 was
selected with some elements of the other two alternatives. The GP Team has developed
the preferred land use alternative and received broad input from the GPAC, community,
and stakeholders (ATTACHMENTS 2 and 3). The GP Team prepared a briefing book
(ATTACHMENT 1) that explained the General Plan process, land use framework,
preferred land use alternative and accompanying land use designations, and more
detailed recommendations for some of the major elements. This briefing book was used
for community engagement as described later in this staff report.

The major elements of the preferred land use alternative are:
    Two Education Districts;
    Two Health and Wellness Districts;
    Regional commercial uses around the Antelope Valley Mall and a regional
  commercial area to the west of the intersection of Palmdale Boulevard/47th Street
  East;
    Mix of employment uses around Plant 42;
    Mixed uses along the Palmdale Boulevard corridor;

  12
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: General Plan Preferred Land Use Alternative
March 16, 2021
Page 4

    Medium density housing, such as low-rise walkups, townhouses, and courtyard
  apartments, south of Palmdale Boulevard; and,
    Village Centers with a mix of neighborhood retail or commercial uses along with
  residential uses in a mixed-use format in various locations throughout the City.

The GP Team also prepared more specific recommendations for the Education Districts,
Health and Wellness Districts, and Village Centers. These are described below and
further illustrated in the briefing book (ATTACHMENT 1).

Education District
The Education District supports a mix of education uses such as trade schools, public
and private higher education facilities, and satellite campuses along with supportive retail,
office, and housing in a campus-like setting. The preferred land use alternative consists
of two education districts:

    Near Antelope Valley Community College and Palmdale High School (west of the
  25th Street East/Palmdale Boulevard intersection)
    Near Palmdale Aerospace Academy  (Palmdale  Boulevard  between
  30th Street East and 40th Street East)

The Education Flex designation is applied to the two districts. The briefing book contains
a sample site plan that illustrates how educational and supportive uses could integrate
with the surrounding neighborhood.

Health and Wellness District
The Health and Wellness District is implemented by the Health and Wellness designation
which supports a mix of public and private medical, health, and wellness uses including
emergency medical facilities, medical and supportive offices, healthcare clinics and
pharmacies. The preferred land use alternative consists of two health and wellness
districts:

    On 10th Street West and Palmdale  Boulevard  around  the  existing
  Palmdale Regional Medical Center; and,
    Next to the Kaiser Permanente facility west of 47th Street East and south of
  Avenue S.

The briefing book has a sample site plan that illustrates how a medical district may
develop over time.

Village Centers and Multi-Use Nodes

  13
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: General Plan Preferred Land Use Alternative
March 16, 2021
Page 5

Village Centers are intended to offer a mix of residential uses and daily goods and
services within residential neighborhoods in a mixed-use setting. Village Centers allow
for the creation of “complete neighborhoods” where residents can access the commercial
and public uses through multiple modes of travel and are connected to the larger
pedestrian and bicycle network.

These centers may consist of a variety of land use designations including:
    Mixed Use 1 (MU1)
    Mixed Use 2 (MU2)
    Neighborhood Commercial (NC)

The preferred land use alternative has Village Centers at the following 11 locations:
    Avenue N and 50th Street West
    Rancho Vista Boulevard and Town Center Drive
    Rancho Vista Boulevard and Seville Avenue
    Ranch Center Drive and Elizabeth Lake Road
    Avenue S and Ranch Center Drive
    Avenue P and 10th Street East
    Avenue Q and 30th Street East
    Palmdale Boulevard and 25th Street East
    Avenue R and 47th Street East
    Avenue S and 25th Street East
    Avenue S and 70th Street East

Multi-Use Nodes are made up primarily commercial uses at higher intensities than the
Village Centers. These nodes offer a mix of uses that attract patrons from across the
City and serve varying needs based on location. The preferred land use alternative has
Multi-Use Nodes at the following five locations:
    Avenue M and Challenger Way
    Sierra Highway and Avenue S
    Palmdale Boulevard and 47th Street East
    Avenue S and 47th Street East
   Fort Tejon Road and Pearblossom Highway
Existing Specific Plans

  14
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: General Plan Preferred Land Use Alternative
March 16, 2021
Page 6

As a part of the preferred land use alternative, four Specific Plans are being rescinded
and replaced with consistent land use designations. The Hillside Residential Specific
Plan and Joshua Hills Estates Specific Plan are both completely built out. Foothill Ranch
Specific Plan and Palmdale Trade and Commerce Specific Plan are also being
re-designated as a part of this process.

Land Use Designations
The GP Team also prepared revised land use designations that accompany the preferred
land use alternative map. These designations contain descriptions of allowed uses,
densities/intensities, and intended character. The proposed designations continue to use
several designations from the 1993 General Plan for the Areas of Stability, i.e., those
areas that are not expected to change.

The land use designations are fully described in the briefing book (ATTACHMENT 1) and
can be divided into the following broad categories:

Residential: There are nine residential designations that cover the range of housing types
expected in Palmdale. Seven of these designations are carried over from the
1993 General Plan. The two new designations address the “missing middle” density
ranges in the City. These new designations allow for housing types that include
townhomes, two to three story walkups, courtyard style multiple-family residential
buildings, mid-rise podium multiple-family residential, etc.

Commercial and Industrial: Six commercial, employment and industrial designations
allow a range of commercial and industrial uses at a variety of scales. The Neighborhood
Commercial and Regional Commercial designations support commercial uses at the
neighborhood and regional scale, respectively. The Visitor Commercial designation
supports retail, entertainment, and hotels to serve the needs of visitors and highway
traffic. The Employment Flex designation covers job-producing uses including offices,
medical, research & development and light industrial uses.

Mixed Use Designations: Mixed use designations allow for a mix of commercial and
residential uses, integrated either in a building (vertical mixed use) or on the same parcel
(horizontal mixed use). Four mixed use designations are proposed at range of densities.

Public Designations: Four designations cover parks, schools, public and civic facilities,
and open space uses.

Specific Plan Designation: This designation covers the existing adopted Specific Plans
in the City. Each Specific Plan document provides more detail about allowed uses,
densities, and other development regulations.

Community Feedback on the Preferred Land Use Alternative
The preferred land use alternative was presented virtually to the community using an
interactive web-based program, called Konveio, that includes an interactive Arc-GIS map,
briefing book, and survey. The briefing book included process and background; major
features of the preferred land use alternative; land use framework map; land use
designations; the preferred land use alternative map; descriptions, examples, and
illustrations for what a Village Center, Health and Wellness District, and Education District
could look like in Palmdale; metrics and comparison of the existing General Plan land
use; and reference maps. Community members were instructed to review the briefing
book and interactive map, then complete a 13-question survey. The English and Spanish
briefing book generated a total of 1,085 views during the engagement period. The survey
was available for five weeks from January 13, 2021, to February 17, 2021, and collected
207 responses (201 English and 6 Spanish). The survey results show a wide diversity of
age ranges as well as a range of racial and ethnic groups.

In general, it is not uncommon to see survey numbers decline while progressing through
the land use alternative development process. In some instances, if a participant is
comfortable with the outcome, they do not bother completing a survey or leaving a
comment. Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that this occurred given that the briefing
book was viewed 1,085 times while only 207 surveys were completed.

While the preferred land use alternative survey received fewer responses than earlier
surveys, overall, respondents clearly indicated a high level of support for the preferred
land use alternative. Seven of the 13 survey questions asked respondents to rate their
level of agreement with the overall preferred land use alternative as well as distinct

of respondents agreed or strongly agreed with the survey statement (ATTACHMENT 2).
Many respondents expressed their excitement for the future of the City and eagerness to

change proposed for either the Westside or Eastside of the City. Some of the comments

    Hope the updated General Plan will bring new employment opportunities to
  Palmdale, while supporting the aerospace presence.
    End inequities and division across Palmdale through the General Plan process.
    Reduce unoccupied buildings and empty lots across the City.
    Offer more housing options at different densities and income levels; housing for
  specific populations like seniors and young professionals and near job centers but
  away from disruptive uses are needed.
    Improve infrastructure by expanding sewer system, bicycle network, sidewalk
  network, and access to recreational trails.
    Promote non-automobile modes of travel while also mitigating traffic impacts from
  proposed development.
    Expand parks, open space, conservation area, and use of shade trees.
    Expand cultural and recreational uses like museums, sports complexes, and
  outdoor amphitheaters.
    Consider a centralized or expanded Education District.
    Address populations that are unhoused and with health disparities; attract a
  second major hospital to Palmdale.

Recommended Changes to the Preferred Land Use Alternative
During the public review of the preferred land use alternative, the GP Team received
several specific comments from the GPAC members, community members, property
owners, and stakeholders. The following changes are considerations for refining the
preferred land use alternative and are illustrated in ATTACHMENT 4.

Health & Wellness Districts
The comments focused on the desire to see a larger health and wellness district on the
Eastside to provide services closer to the residents in this area. In addition, several other
uses were also recommended for this district. As such, the GP Team recommends the
following revisions to the preferred land use alternative:
    Expand the Medical District at Avenue S and 47th Street East to 46 acres
    Expand allowed uses to include:

 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: General Plan Preferred Land Use Alternative
March 16, 2021
Page 10

  o Senior housing
  o Assisted living and supportive care uses
  o Educational/vocational training facilities

Education Districts
Several GPAC members suggested that the preferred land use alternative should
consider reserving land for a large four-year college campus instead of, or in addition to,
the two proposed education districts. The two proposed locations are within a mile of
each other along Palmdale Boulevard and range from 40 to 60 acres. Other comments
also included the desire to see an education district on the Westside. As such, the
GP Team recommends the following revisions to the preferred land use alternative:
    Designate approximately 110 acres at the northwest corner of Palmdale Boulevard
  and 47th Street East as Education Flex.
    Adjust surrounding designations to address this change including redesignate the
  Education District at Palmdale Boulevard and 35th Street East (next to the
  Palmdale Aerospace Academy) with mixed use designations.
    Allow education-related uses in the Health and Wellness Districts to allow for
  vocational training uses in the area surrounding the Palmdale Regional Medical
  Center.

Area surrounding Plant 42
Several property owners and aerospace industry representatives requested limiting
incompatible uses within the Accident Potential Zones (APZ) for Plant 42 as delineated
in the Plant 42 Air Installation Compatible Use Zone (AICUZ) Study. Upon
reconsideration, the GP Team recommends further limiting residential uses within the
APZ as follows:
    Designate land within APZ 2 between Rancho Vista Boulevard, Technology Drive,
  Division Street and Sierra Highway as Employment Flex and Industrial.

During the outreach period, the public reviewed and provided feedback on the preferred
land use alternative and suggested several changes as noted above. In addition to public
feedback, obtaining input on the preferred land use alternative from the
Planning Commission and City Council is also an important piece of the preferred land
use alternative development process. As such, in addition to providing a summary of the
public feedback on the preferred land use alternative and an update on the General Plan
process, the GP Team is also asking for the City Council to review the preferred land use
alternative, the requested changes, and provide feedback. After receiving input from the
Planning Commission and City Council, the GP Team will implement final adjustments
and finalize the General Plan land use map.

The education districts will center around existing educational uses and attract similar trade schools, adult schools,  VILLAGE CENTERS:

walkable campus setting with support services including retail and some residential and hospitality.  employees, and visitors to easily access. These centers are smaller and more walkable than other commercial centers
  and are typically located in or near residential neighborhoods.

Both health and wellness districts build off existing medical centers including the Palmdale Regional Medical Center  MULTI-USE NODES:
and Kaiser Permanente Palmdale Medical Offices. This district encourages other medical and support services to locate  The multi-use nodes are made up primarily of commercial uses in a similar but at a higher intensity than the village
in close proximity. Private and public medical offices, clinics, other healthcare and/or wellness uses are recommended  centers. These nodes offer a mix of uses that attract patrons from across Palmdale and serve varying needs based on

   City Council Staff Report
DATE:  MARCH 16, 2021
TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL
FROM:  CITY ATTORNEY’S OFFICE
DISTRICT:  ALL
SUBJECT:  VEHICLE ALLOWANCES

ISSUE
Review and discuss City Council Vehicle Allowances.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Discuss the current City Council authorized vehicle allowance; and
  2. Provide direction to Staff regarding possible changes to the vehicle allowance.

BACKGROUND
The City Council is authorized, pursuant to Palmdale Municipal Code Section 2.08.070,
to “receive a vehicle allowance, at the end of each calendar month, without the necessity
of presentation of an itemized accounting, receipts, vouchers or other documentation.”
The amount of the vehicle allowance is set by resolution of the City Council and must be
“reasonably related to what is required for the performance of the City Councilmembers’
public duties.” The current vehicle allowance, established in March 2001, is $200 per
month. At the March 2nd City Council meeting, the Mayor expressed some concern that
the current amount of the vehicle allowance was not justified considering reduced City
Council travel during the COVID-19 pandemic. Staff was directed to prepare this report.

DISCUSSION
State law authorizes cities to adopt vehicle allowances for city councilmembers.
Specifically, California Government Code Section 1223 provides that, “[w]hen traveling
expenses are allowed by law to any state, county, judicial district, or city officer, he may
contract with the appropriate authorities for an allowance or mileage rate for the use of
vehicles owned or rented and used by him in the performance of duty, in lieu of the usual
transportation charges.”

In 1989, the City Council adopted Ordinance 829, establishing a $100 per month vehicle
allowance. The vehicle allowance was subsequently increased to $200, effective March
1, 2001. In 2005, the California legislature adopted AB 1234 which, among other things,

in the performance of their duties. Specifically, California Government Code Section
53232.2 authorizes reimbursement for “actual and necessary expenses incurred in the
performance of official duties,” and requires local agencies to adopt a reimbursement
policy. In addition, California Government Code Section 53232.3 requires City
Councilmembers to submit expense reports, with receipts evidencing incurred
expenses, prior to being reimbursed by the City.

When the City Council adopted the required reimbursement policy, it asked the City
Attorney’s Office if vehicle allowances were still permissible in light of the new rules
allowing reimbursement only after submittal of an expense report identifying “actual and
necessary expenses” already incurred by a City Councilmember “in the performance of
official duties.” The City Attorney’s Office opined that vehicle allowances were still
permissible and not prohibited by AB 1234. However, there was no direct authority on
the issue and that some city attorneys were advising their clients that vehicle allowances
were no longer permissible. In response to this advice, the City Council directed our
office to seek an opinion from the California Attorney General. On February 18, 2010,
the Attorney General issued an opinion that concluded “a city may provide a vehicle
allowance to its city council members in lieu of reimbursing actual vehicle expenses after
such expenses are incurred.” A copy of the Attorney General Opinion is attached to this
report.

While the existing vehicle allowance is legal, the Palmdale Municipal Code requires the
vehicle allowance to be “reasonably related to what is required for the performance of
the City Councilmembers’ public duties.” If the City Council believes that the amount of
$200 no longer reflects the reasonable monthly cost to use a personal vehicle for City
Council business, the City Council could:
  1. Direct staff to bring back a resolution temporarily changing the amount of the
  vehicle allowance for a specific period of time (e.g., until the declared emergency
  relating to the COVID-19 pandemic is terminated);
  2. Direct staff to bring back a resolution permanently changing the amount of the
  vehicle allowance; or
  3. Direct staff to bring back an ordinance repealing the authorized vehicle
  allowance. Reimbursement for vehicle use would be subject to the City Council
  Expense Reimbursement Policy.

If the City Council believes that the amount of $200 continues to reflect the reasonable
monthly cost to use a personal vehicle for City Council business, the City Council need
not take any action.

  May a city provide a vehicle allowance to its city council members in lieu of

reimbursing actual vehicle expenses after such expenses are incurred.

  We are asked whether a city may provide a vehicle allowance to members of its
city council, rather than reimbursing the members for their actual vehicle expenses. The
main difference between a vehicle allowance and a vehicle expense reimbursement is that
an allowance is paid out in regular, pre-determined installments, while a reimbursement
is paid out after an expense has been incurred, and in an amount corresponding to the
actual expense.

central to our inquiry.1 Section 1223 permits city council members to contract directly
with the city for a vehicle allowance when the council members’ travel expenses are
allowed by law.2 Section 53232.2 establishes requirements for reimbursement of city
council members’ travel expenses,3 and section 53232.3 requires that expense report

ISSUE
Provide response to the City Council’s inquiry about changing the terms of office for the
Mayor position from two to four years; modifying the Mayoral position from “Elected-at-
Large” to rotating amongst Council Members and seek direction regarding the formation
of a redistricting commission.

RECOMMENDATION
  1. Receive and file report regarding the City Council’s inquiry on changing the terms
  of office for the Mayoral position and provide direction to staff on which
  modification, if any, they prefer.

  2. Provide a recommendation to staff regarding the formation of a redistricting
  commission considering the following options:

  a) Whether to appoint an independent districting commission or some other
  redistricting commission;
  b) Clarify requirements to serve on the redistricting commission;
  c) Establish how many residents should be on commission;
  d) Establish selection process;
  e) Provide input on community outreach.

BACKGROUND
On March 2, 2021, redistricting and the formation of a committee was presented to the
City Council for consideration. The City Council directed staff to bring back the item for
further discussion at a workshop. Moreover, the City Council directed staff to provide
information on additional items:

  1. Modifying the Mayoral position from two years, to fours years; and,

Election of Mayor and Number Council of Districts
While the Charter of the City of Palmdale provides the designation of the Council-
Manager Form of Government (Article 2, Section 200), describes election powers of the
City (Article 6, Section 600) and procedures for Amendment to the Charter (Article 8,
Section 800), it is the Palmdale Municipal Code that governs and describes both our
council districts and the process of electing a Mayor. (Palmdale Municipal Code §
2.08.010). Pursuant to Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC) Section 2.08.010 the office of the
Mayor of the City shall be an elective office which shall have a term of two years, and
there shall be a citywide election to such office. (Ord. 1471 § 1, 2015; Ord. 1357 § 1,
2008). Government Code Section 34900 provides that in cities presently having elected
mayors, the city council may also submit to the electors the question of whether the mayor
shall thereafter serve a two-year or four-year term.

Thus, if it is the intention of the Council (on an Ordinance to be returned at a future date),
the question of whether a Mayor should: 1) serve a term of two or four years, or 2) be a
rotating mayor selected by the Council, rather than by the electors at-large, can be
submitted to the electors at a regularly scheduled election.

If there is direction from the Council to set forth a matter abolishing the Mayor-at-large
election, and an Ordinance or vote of the electors is brought to that effect, it will have a
significant impact on districts and redistricting.

If the direction is to move to a rotating Mayor system, then the Mayor-at-large seat as the
fifth Council member would cease to exist, and it would require the addition of a fifth
Council seat, via a fifth district, which would need to be reviewed and included in the
course of re-districting. Likewise, we would need to amend PMC Section 2.08.020 “City
Council” which states, “The Mayor shall be elected on a Citywide basis and the four
Councilmembers shall be elected from four geographic districts in which each
resides by a vote of the electors in each respective district.”

Staff is seeking direction from the Council as to which, if any, modification they deem
necessary and appropriate.

ISSUE

  4. Establish selection process;
  5. Provide input on community outreach.

BACKGROUND
The California Voting Rights Act (“CVRA”) was enacted to implement the California
constitutional guarantees of equal protection and the right to vote. The purpose of the
CVRA is to prevent an at-large election system from diluting minority voting power and
impairing underrepresented groups from influencing the outcome of a race. While
modeled after the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965 (“FVRA”)1, the CVRA lowers the
threshold required to establish a voting rights violation. The CVRA made fundamental
changes to voting rights in California, making it easier for plaintiffs in California to
challenge at-large voting systems which can dilute the voting power of underrepresented
groups.

Page 2

The City Council adopted Ordinance 1471 transitioning from at-large to by-district city
councilmember elections under Elections Code § 10010. Once the federal census is
completed and released, State law requires the City Council to review and adjust the
boundaries of its districts to ensure compliance with the Voting Rights Act.

Two new laws have been enacted since the City Council transitioned to district elections,
which govern the redistricting process.

  1. SB 1018 became effective on January 1, 2019 expanding the methods for re-
  drawing district maps. Under this legislation, in addition to appointing an advisory,
  or an independent commission, the City Council may instead elect to appoint a
  hybrid commission or contract with Los Angeles County’s Citizen Redistricting
  Commission (“CRC”).

  2. The Fair Maps Act (AB 849) became effective January 1, 2020 and created
  standardized redistricting criteria aimed to keep communities together and to
  prohibit partisan gerrymandering. The Act also expanded community outreach
  and public hearing requirements and timelines, which coincide with the State
  redistricting schedule (Attachment 1).

DISCUSSION
The redistricting process is important in ensuring that each City Councilmember
represents approximately the same number of constituents. A professional
demographer will assist the City to create proposed district boundaries with suggestions
and feedback from the community. Residents will be able to provide input on boundaries
and suggested criteria for creating boundaries. The process will be transparent and
accessible to all residents. Ultimately, the City Council adopts an ordinance establishing
district boundaries.

State law also requires the City Council to adopt district boundaries using specific
criteria as set forth in the following order of priority:
  1. To the extent practicable, city council districts shall be geographically contiguous.
  Areas that meet only at the points of adjoining corners are not contiguous.
  2. To the extent practicable, the geographic integrity of any local neighborhood or
  local community of interest shall be respected in a manner that minimizes its
  division.
  a. A “community of interest” is a population that shares common social or
  economic interests that should be included within a single district for
  purposes of its effective and fair representation. Communities of interest
  do not include relationships with political parties, incumbents, or political
  candidates.

  108
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Report for 2021 Redistricting Program
March 2, 2021
Page 3

  3. City Council district boundaries should be easily identifiable and understandable
  by residents. To the extent practicable, city council districts shall be bounded by
  natural and artificial barriers, by streets, or by the boundaries of the city.
  4. To the extent practicable, and where it does not conflict with the preceding
  criteria in this subdivision, city council districts shall be drawn to encourage
  geographical compactness in a manner that nearby areas of population are not
  bypassed in favor of more distant populations.

State law does not allow council district boundaries to be drawn for the purpose of favoring
or discriminating against a political party. SB 1018 provides additional methods for
adjusting boundaries (Attachment 1 provides for detailed information for each
commission):
  1. the City Council may adopt districts itself;
  2. the City Council may appoint an advisory commission to recommend district
  boundaries for City Council adoption (ex. San Jose, Anaheim, Pasadena);
  3. the City Council may establish an independent redistricting commission to
  either adopt or recommend new boundaries to the City Council (Long Beach, Los
  Angeles, Sacramento); and
  4. the City Council may establish a hybrid redistricting commission to either adopt
  or recommend new boundaries to the City Council (ex. Chula Vista).

The descriptions below provide a brief summary of the types of commissions and
Attachment 2 provides more detailed information.

Advisory Commission
The process for establishing an advisory commission is like other local boards and
commissions. The commission shall consist of residents and the City may specify the
qualifications and selection process for commissioners. Current City Councilmembers or
family, staff member or paid campaign staff of a City Council member may not serve on
the commission.

Independent Commissions
State law authorizes the City Council to transfer redistricting authority to an independent
redistricting commission. The manner of appointment is set by the City Council, but
commissioners cannot be appointed directly by the City Council. Commissioners must
pass an extensive list of possible disqualifications and there are post-service limitations
on their ability to run for local office, serve on a local board or commission, seek city
employment, or otherwise contract with the City.

Hybrid Commissions
A hybrid commission is formed in a manner like an independent commission and has
similar preservice and post-service limitations, but a hybrid commission is required to

submit two or more maps to the City Council and the City Council must select one of the
submitted maps. The City Council is not permitted to alter the selected map in any way
except as needed to comply with federal or State law.

Committee Member Appointments
There are different methods for selecting commissioners as described below:
  1. City Council appointment - Each Councilmember may appoint one member
  from their district following an publicly advertised application process.
  2. Independent appointment - After an open application process, a selection
  body, which is independent of the governing board, appoints the commissioners.
  3. Random draw and commission appointment - After an open application
  process, staff will remove ineligible applicants and create a sub-pool of the most
  qualified candidates. A subset of commissioners is selected at random from that
  sub-pool. This method follows the model of the State Redistricting Commission
  and is intended to prevent the governing board from influencing who serves on the
  commission. Some ordinances require or encourage geographic or ethnic diversity
  on the commission. Many ordinances require prospective commissioners to meet
  certain eligibility qualifications, generally to ensure their political independence
  from incumbent officeholders. For example, incumbents and recent candidates for
  political office, as well as their family members and employees, are often prohibited
  from serving on the commission.

Public Hearings and Community Outreach
Before adopting a final map, the City Council must hold at least four (4) public hearings
to provide input regarding the composition of one or more City Council district. These
hearings shall consist of:
  •  At least one public hearing before the City Council draws draft map(s.) This
  hearing may be conducted by City staff, a consultant, or a redistricting
  commission.
  •  At least two public hearings after the City Council have drawn draft map(s).
  •  At least one public hearing or public workshop shall be held on a Saturday, on a
  Sunday or after 6 p.m. on a weekday Monday through Friday.
